ideas.title: I Tested Every Popular Day Trading Strategy. Your Favorite Is Dead.
ideas.name: Opening range breakout, 30 minute box, Nasdaq futures
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures (one NQ contract); also tested on nine other futures markets, gold was runner-up
ideas.entry: Wait 30 minutes after the 9:30 New York open, mark the high and low of that box. A close above the box is a buy, a close below is a sell. One trade a day. Bar size used for the close test is unstated.
ideas.exit: Stop on the opposite side of the box. Otherwise hold until the market closes. No target.
ideas.filters: none in the base version (see C-02 and C-03 for filters)
ideas.sizing: one contract; the micro Nasdaq contract (one tenth size) is suggested to shrink drawdown
ideas.claimed_results: Search: 10 futures markets, 1-minute bars 2020-2026 (6.6 million bars), nine famous strategies, a thousand settings, 3.58 million trades, 1,200 backtests, real commissions and slippage (amounts unstated). Settings chosen on 2020-2023, frozen, judged on 2024-2026. Nasdaq ORB total +96,825 on one contract over 2020-2026; positive in each year 2021 to 2025; about two thirds of its settings profitable on the unseen years; survived four times the slippage. Loses on about 52 percent of days. Normal days (two in three) lost 848,780, trend days made 945,605. Best 10 percent of trades made about nine times the total profit. Average win 2,208, average loss 1,891. About 89 percent of profit came from the long side; shorts roughly flat and losing in the last two years. 9 April 2025 alone +34,240. Worst drawdown 93,465 on NQ (9,410 on micro). Once lost seven months in a row and nine days in a row. 2026 year to date -59,555, and at recording it was 93,465 down since June. On gold, one extra tick of slippage turned it into a loser.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Intraday bars (1-minute ideal, 5-minute workable) for NQ or a Nasdaq proxy covering 2020-2026 with correct session times, plus a cost model. Yahoo gives no intraday history. Daily bars cannot place a 30 minute box.
ideas.red_flags: One survivor out of a thousand, on one market, in a mostly bull decade (author says so himself). Commission and slippage values are not given. Whole edge sits in rare trend days, so a short sample would mislead. Dollar results are for one contract with no percentage return. Author frames it as a candidate that still needs a forward test.
ideas.why_priority: The only strategy in this folder that survived a frozen out-of-sample judge and a cost stress, with near-complete rules, but we cannot test it without intraday data.

ideas.title: I Tested Every Popular Day Trading Strategy. Your Favorite Is Dead.
ideas.name: ORB version two: long side only, skip Mondays
ideas.entry: As C-01 but buys only; no trade on Mondays
ideas.filters: long only; skip Mondays. Both rules chosen using only information up to end of 2023
ideas.sizing: one contract; micro contract for survivability
ideas.claimed_results: On the unseen 2024-2026 years: profit rose from 34,675 to 39,415 with fewer trades; worst drawdown fell from 93,465 to 38,260 (3,840 on the micro). 2026 year to date -13,055 versus -59,555 for the original. Still loses money in more than four months out of ten. The Monday weakness showed up in both 2020-2023 and 2024-2026. Small opening range and big gap filters flip-flopped between the two periods and were judged noise.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Same as C-01 (intraday NQ bars). A bare Monday effect can be checked on daily bars, but that is not the same claim as an ORB losing on Mondays.
ideas.red_flags: The Monday rule was found by looking at five weekdays and keeping the one that looked bad twice, which the author admits could be chance. Long-only is a bet that the bull market continues. Improvement is still a loss in 2026.
ideas.why_priority: Cheap add-on to C-01 but the Monday filter is a one-in-five look and long-only is regime dependent.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: News-day switch: stand aside on Fed, inflation and jobs days for breakout strategies
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures; effect compared across the thousand-setting study on 10 futures markets
ideas.entry: Applies to a host strategy (the opening range breakout). Host entry as C-01.
ideas.exit: Applies to a host strategy; no separate exit
ideas.filters: No trade on the 210 event days: 52 Fed decisions, 80 inflation reports, 78 jobs reports since 2020
ideas.claimed_results: ORB lost 52,270 over about 200 news days and made roughly 149,095 on all other days (transcript text is garbled, but 96,825 plus 52,270 gives 149,095). Skipping news days lifts the total from 96,825 to about 149,095. Lost on news days in six of seven years; fewer than two in 100 random sets of 200 ordinary days were as bad. Across the thousand settings, mean-reversion types (VWAP fade, RSI, Bollinger reversal) did better on news days in 70 to 78 percent of settings; ORB and gap fill did worse on news days in 62 and 70 percent respectively (order as spoken).
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Intraday bars to run the host strategy, plus a verified economic calendar. The calendar part is free (Fed site dates; jobs and inflation dates need another route because the video says the statistics agency blocks automated downloads). A daily-bar version would be a different test: split our own RSI(5) trades by whether they straddle an event day.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: none directly; the daily analogue would act on the systems book (RSI(5) on nine ETFs)
ideas.red_flags: About 200 events, one host strategy, 2022 dominates several event results (author says so). Author notes his random-basket tests do not fully correct for how many questions he asked.
ideas.why_priority: Clear on/off rule with a stated control, but needs intraday data; its daily analogue is a derived test, not something the video ran.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Jobs-report fade held to the 9:30 cash open
ideas.entry: Jobs report is released at 8:30 New York. Wait five minutes, then trade against the direction of those five minutes. How the five-minute direction is measured (open to close of the window) is unstated.
ideas.exit: Hold until 9:30 when the regular stock market opens. Exits after 15 or 30 minutes lost in every variant tried.
ideas.filters: Jobs reports only. Does not work for inflation reports or Fed decisions.
ideas.sizing: one contract; two points of slippage per side plus commission (commission amount unstated)
ideas.claimed_results: 75 jobs reports: +22,795 (profitable in six of seven years and in both halves of the sample). Control: same trade at 8:30 on days with no release, drawn 10,000 times; median result -7,375; two of 10,000 baskets did as well. Double slippage (four points per side): +16,795. Eight points per side: +4,795. Waiting 1, 3, 10 or 15 minutes instead of five also works if the hold is about an hour. Author calls it a lead, not proof, and recommends a small forward test.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: 1-minute NQ (or ES) futures bars including the 8:30 to 9:30 pre-open session, 2020 onward (longer is better), plus verified jobs report dates. Not available from Yahoo daily bars. Video says its 10-market minute dataset cost about 75 dollars in total, vendor not named.
ideas.red_flags: Only 75 events. Found after asking many questions of the same data; the random-basket test does not correct for that, and the author says so. Fills at 8:35 on a data release can be much worse than the slippage assumed. 2022 is an outlier year for several results. Reason given for the reversal (thin liquidity before the cash open) is an interpretation he says he cannot prove.
ideas.why_priority: Complete rule, a proper luck control and a cost stress, but a small sample and no free data to test it.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Fed decision day return and pre-Fed drift
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures as stated (daily proxies would be QQQ, SPY, ^NDX, ^GSPC)
ideas.entry: unstated (the drift is described as stocks rising over the 24 hours before the decision; no trade rule given)
ideas.filters: Fed decision dates only (52 decisions since 2020)
ideas.claimed_results: Nasdaq averaged +0.36 percent on Fed decision days; about one in eight random samples of ordinary days matched that. The pre-Fed drift over the 24 hours before the decision was visible but about one in ten random samples matched it, and it lost money in 2025 and 2026. Author's verdict: not a proven edge.
ideas.red_flags: Only 52 events. Return basis (close to close, open to close) is unstated. The announcement is at 2pm, so a daily bar cannot isolate the 24 hours before it exactly; a daily proxy blurs the claim. Fed dates from the Fed site are free, but we must write the calendar ourselves.
ideas.why_priority: A stated number with a random-sample comparison, checkable on decades of free daily ETF history instead of his 52 events; pre-register the definition before running.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Jobs-report Friday weakness
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures as stated (daily proxies: QQQ, ^NDX)
ideas.entry: unstated (an observation, not a trade rule)
ideas.filters: Jobs report days versus other Fridays without a release
ideas.claimed_results: On 74 jobs report days the Nasdaq returned -0.25 percent on average versus +0.06 percent on other Fridays; only 1.7 percent of random sets of ordinary Fridays were as weak. Negative in 2020, 2022, 2025 and 2026, positive in 2021, 2023 and 2024; fewer than half of jobs days were actually down, so a handful of big sell-offs drive the average. Author says it is not an edge.
ideas.red_flags: Tiny sample, average driven by a few days, return basis unstated, and the author himself labels it newsletter-grade seasonality. The jobs report date list is the awkward part because the statistics agency blocks automated downloads.
ideas.why_priority: Cheap to run on 25 plus years of daily data, and a good test of whether a post-2020 calendar quirk is just a short-sample accident.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Event-day range expansion as a risk or sizing input
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures as stated; cross-market reaction also given for Russell, Treasuries, euro, yen, gold, oil
ideas.entry: not a trade; an observation about size of move
ideas.filters: Fed decision, jobs and inflation report days
ideas.claimed_results: Typical Nasdaq daily move about 55 percent larger on Fed and jobs days than on days without a release, about 10 percent larger on inflation days. First five minutes after the 210 releases are about 0.04 percent of minutes but carry 2.3 percent of Nasdaq variance since 2020. Reaction size shifts by regime: first 15 minutes after an inflation report moved the Nasdaq about 0.16 percent in 2020, 1.78 percent in 2022, 0.3 to 0.4 percent since. First 5 minute reaction in multiples of normal: inflation hits Nasdaq and Russell about 2.5 times; Fed hits euro, yen and 10-year Treasuries about 4.5 times, stocks about 2 times, gold over 3 times; oil barely moves.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Could feed the volatility sizing in P-0084 (trend following, 28-market ETF portfolio)
ideas.red_flags: Descriptive only; nothing says reducing size on event days improves risk-adjusted return. Basis of the daily move (range or absolute return) is unstated.
ideas.why_priority: True and easy to check on daily bars, but it is a volatility fact, not a return edge, and it only matters for sizing.

ideas.title: I Let AI Build the Most Complicated Trading System Possible
ideas.name: Quarterly exam gate: sit in cash unless the strategy passed the past year
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures as tested; the gate itself is market independent
ideas.entry: Host strategy trades only in a quarter that follows a passed exam
ideas.exit: Host strategy exits as normal; if the exam is failed it sits out the next three months in cash
ideas.filters: Exam: prove yourself on the past year. The pass criterion (profit, Sharpe, anything else) is unstated.
ideas.claimed_results: 15 quarters, 2023 to 2026: it traded in 9 and failed its own exam in 6. It stayed out of April to June 2025, the tariff crash quarter, in which an ungated simple rule lost 28,560. Over the whole period the AI committee with all four changes (volatility-sized stops, same five entry times, trade only when expected profit clears a bar, quarterly exam) ended at +170 on 264 trades while the coin flip lost 179,805, the one-line rule lost 147,180 and buying every slot lost 85,390. Contribution of the exam alone is not separated from the other three changes.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Could be run as an overlay on the RSI(5) systems book and on P-0084
ideas.red_flags: Version two was run on history the author had already seen, so it is not blind. Only 264 trades; he says the uncertainty range includes zero. The exam alone is not isolated from three other changes. Equity-curve gating often just lags.
ideas.why_priority: A meta-rule we can test on daily strategies we already run, but it needs a pass criterion fixed in advance and the evidence in the video is thin.

ideas.title: I Let AI Build the Most Complicated Trading System Possible
ideas.name: Machine-learning timing filter ('bouncer'): model decides when to stay out, a dumb rule picks direction
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures, using features from 10 futures markets plus VIX
ideas.entry: Gradient boosted tree model on 765 numeric features (69 Nasdaq itself, 660 cross-market, 17 regime, 19 volatility) forecasts the next hour's Nasdaq move. Version one trades if the forecast beats twice the trading cost; version two adds volatility-sized stops, five fixed entry times and a quarterly exam. The direction twist: follow the last 30 minutes at the moments the model chose. Stop multiple and the required profit bar are unstated.
ideas.exit: Hold one hour; version two has volatility-scaled stops (multiple unstated)
ideas.filters: Trade only when expected profit after costs clears a bar; quarterly exam (see C-08)
ideas.claimed_results: Version one trained 2020-2024, frozen, judged on 20 unseen months of 2025-2026: -145,575 (1,254 trades; 88 percent of coin-flip versions with the same timing did better; costs alone 56,430 at 45 per trade; before costs -89,145). A plain linear model was the only profitable one at +9,995; trees on Nasdaq data only -86,075; plus other markets -79,940; plus mood -37,050; two most complex systems -145,575 and -154,360. Most confident 10 percent of trades (126) lost 76,735, right only 46.8 percent. Version two (not blind): +170 on 264 trades, all buys, under 4 percent at the 10:01 open versus 20 percent of the chances, average stop 67 points versus 87 on skipped moments. Following the last 30 minutes at the model's 264 moments: +10,900; the same rule at all other moments: -155,655. A one-line version (buy at 11, 12, 1 or 2 when calmer than usual) lost 60,135 over 1,655 trades.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: 1-minute futures bars for ten markets plus VIX from 2020, a feature pipeline and a gradient boosting library. Video says the data cost about 75 dollars; vendor not named. A daily-bar version would be a different, untested design.
ideas.red_flags: Version two only breaks even and was tuned on seen history. 264 trades, interval spans zero, found looking backwards (author says all of this). Very heavy for a lead that the author says the model could not turn into direction skill.
ideas.why_priority: Heavy build on data we lack for a break-even result; the useful part is the timing-versus-direction split, which we can copy as a method.

ideas.title: This Trading Strategy Made $267,715. Then I Tried to Destroy It.
ideas.name: Morning-momentum continuation, 10:30 in, 3:55 out
ideas.entry: At 10:30 New York, if yesterday's range was above a volatility threshold (value unstated) and the Nasdaq has moved away from the open by more than a threshold (value unstated; later hindsight values 0.15 and 0.2 are quoted without units), buy if up, sell if down. One trade a day.
ideas.exit: Out at 3:55 pm, nothing overnight; no stop is stated (none was added for the frozen test)
ideas.sizing: one contract; 45 dollars model cost per round trip
ideas.claimed_results: Picked from 20,976 configurations, ranked by the weaker of the discovery and validation results. 2020-2023 +177,960, then +89,755 in validation: total 267,715, profit factor 1.3, 962 trades, Sharpe 1.22, win rate 56 percent, six positive calendar periods in a row, every year positive 2020 to early 2025 (2022 especially strong). Survived doubled costs (90 per trade) and nearby thresholds on the old sample. Then frozen and run forward 340 sessions (246 trades): -38,735, Sharpe -0.56, profit factor under 1, max drawdown 73,770. Re-tuning the threshold afterwards (0.15 about +27,000, 0.2 about +55,000) is called a trap because that data had by then become research data.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: 1-minute (or 30-minute) NQ bars with open, 10:30 and 3:55 prices, 2020 onward. A daily-bar stand-in cannot see the 10:30 move.
ideas.red_flags: It failed the frozen test; the video exists to show that. 20,976 configurations searched. Two thresholds left unstated. Not worth testing as a strategy.
ideas.why_priority: Failed its own frozen judgement and we lack the data; keep it as a worked example of the method, not as a rule to test.

ideas.title: I Let AI Build the Most Complicated Trading System Possible
ideas.name: One-line rule: follow the last 30 minutes, hold an hour
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures, one contract (20 dollars a point)
ideas.entry: At 10:01, if the first half hour rose, buy; if it fell, sell. The other entry times are described only as the same five times; a later passage mentions 11, 12, 1 and 2 as times to buy in a different one-liner.
ideas.sizing: one contract; 45 dollars per trade (commission plus a point of slippage each way)
ideas.claimed_results: Lost 28,515 over the 20 unseen months (the transcript digits are slightly garbled). On the later 15-quarter run it lost 147,180 and traded through the April to June 2025 quarter for a 28,560 loss. Coin flip with same timing lost 88,005 on the first run and 179,805 on the later one; buying every slot lost 85,390. Author's remark: day trading the Nasdaq hour by hour is a meat grinder after costs.
ideas.red_flags: Lost on every cut shown. Entry-time list not fully stated.
ideas.why_priority: A losing benchmark, not an idea; useful only as a baseline for intraday filters.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Fed press-conference reversal (2:30 pm move versus 2:00 pm statement)
ideas.entry: unstated (only an observation, no trade rule)
ideas.claimed_results: Across 52 decisions the 2:30 pm press conference produced the larger move 73 percent of the time, typically twice as large, and went the opposite way in nearly half of cases. First five minutes after a release matched the next hour's direction only 47 percent (inflation), 48 percent (Fed) and 40 percent (jobs); correlation about -0.3 for jobs reports and Fed decisions, so big first moves tend to be partly taken back. In the median event 86 percent of the first five minutes of movement is over inside the first minute.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Minute bars across 2:00 to 3:30 pm on Fed days; a trade rule would also need to be defined by us.
ideas.red_flags: No rule, 52 events, descriptive statistics only.
ideas.why_priority: A hint about overshoot on Fed days, but there is no rule and no data to test one.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Headline reaction scalp: trade the first-minute direction after a release
ideas.entry: Watch the first minute after the release, enter in that direction at the next minute's open
ideas.filters: all three event types combined (208 events)
ideas.sizing: one contract; slippage per side tried at 1, 4 and 8 points
ideas.claimed_results: 1 point of slippage: -24,765 over 208 events; 4 points: -49,725; 8 points: about -83,000 (digits garbled in the transcript). No slippage assumption made it profitable.
ideas.red_flags: Negative result; author notes minute bars cannot show who wins the first seconds.
ideas.why_priority: Lost under every cost assumption, so there is nothing to test.

ideas.title: He Wins 90% of His Trades. I Have Bad News.
ideas.name: Pivot support and resistance scalp, 5 point target, 25 point stop
ideas.markets: USTEC / Nasdaq 100 futures (tested on the micro: 2 dollars a point)
ideas.entry: On the 1-minute chart, a pivot high is a candle whose high is above the 10 candles before and the 10 after (pivot low mirrored). Each pivot becomes a level, tradeable only after the 10 right-hand candles have closed. Price returning to a support level is a buy, to a resistance level a sell. Each level trades once on the first touch, one position at a time, contract roll days skipped.
ideas.exit: Take profit 5 points, stop loss 25 points. If a candle hits both, counted as a loss.
ideas.sizing: one micro contract (10 dollars to win, 50 to lose)
ideas.claimed_results: Commenter claimed 89 to 91 percent wins over 300 plus trades with a maximum losing streak of five. Break-even win rate 83.3 percent. Test over 2020 to 5 Oct 2026, 2.4 million candles, 97,169 trades: win rate 81.3 percent; -120,010 before costs, 129,587 costs, -249,597 net; lost in every year. Random entries with same bracket (200,000 trials) won 83.0 percent. 10/50 bracket: 82.8 percent against 83.3 break-even. 2/10: 73.3 percent. 5/5: 43.6 percent pivots versus 47.2 random. 25 target/5 stop: 16.3 percent against 16.7 break-even. Best month 86 percent; September 2026 79.6 percent; only 0.3 percent of 300-trade windows reached 89 percent; real maximum losing streak nine. With optimistic ordering inside the entry candle the win rate jumps to 92.5 percent (78 of 82 months at 89 percent or more); 65.7 percent of optimistic wins happen inside the entry candle; proven wins only: 81.5 percent.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: 1-minute NQ bars (tick data to settle same-candle order).
ideas.red_flags: The claim is refuted by the video. The reproduced numbers sit between the pessimistic and optimistic fill orders, so the claimed result most likely comes from candle-order optimism.
ideas.why_priority: Debunked; the lesson (break-even win rate, random entry control, pessimistic bar order) is the product, not the strategy.

ideas.title: I Tested Every Popular Day Trading Strategy. Your Favorite Is Dead.
ideas.name: Classic intraday indicator set killed by costs (EMA crossover, RSI reversal, Bollinger bands, VWAP fade, gap fill, ICT silver bullet, power hour)
ideas.entry: unstated (parameters and rules for each of the nine strategies are not given; only eight are named)
ideas.claimed_results: EMA crossover: about a million trades, around 50 cents of edge per trade against about 26 dollars of cost. RSI reversal: right about 60 percent of the time yet lost money. ICT silver bullet: about 5 dollars a trade against 25 dollars of costs. VWAP fade, gap fill and Bollinger bands lost (no numbers). Power hour: +122,990 on the selection years, then -42,390 on the unseen years.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: 1-minute futures bars for several markets, plus rules and parameters that the video does not give. Daily-bar versions of EMA crossover and RSI are different tests and are partly covered by P-0082.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: EMA crossover overlaps the Davey golden cross we tested; RSI reversal overlaps the RSI(2) and RSI(5) tests. Those were intraday futures with costs, not daily ETFs.
ideas.red_flags: No rules or parameters, so nothing to replicate. The point is cost versus edge per trade on intraday data. The daily versions are not what he tested.
ideas.why_priority: A graveyard list with no rules; use it only as a reminder to compute edge per trade against cost per trade.

frameworks.name: Freeze, then judge once; rank by the weaker period
frameworks.what_it_is: Search many configurations on a discovery window, require a minimum trade count, then rank survivors by the worse of the discovery and validation scores (so a strong period cannot hide a weak one). After choosing, freeze every parameter and run one forward block of fresh data with no new filter, stop or regime rule. If it fails, do not retune against that block, because it has become research data. Also show the frozen block separately from the full history, since the full curve can stay profitable while the frozen test fails. The same selected-then-frozen split (2020-2023 pick, 2024-2026 judge) is used in 8wJQrfn_otM and wed-hztsQlQ.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: For P-0084 and the RSI(5) systems book: choose parameters on one window, rank by the weaker of two sub-periods, write the frozen spec into the pre-registration commit, and report the judged block on its own line. Count the configurations searched in each P-number so the trial count is public.

frameworks.name: Same-trade random control baskets
frameworks.what_it_is: Run the identical trade (same clock time, same hold, same cost) on randomly chosen non-event days 10,000 times and report where the real result falls. Related versions: random entries with the same stop and target (200,000 trials, snZ89tkMFoA); a coin picks buy or sell at the system's own entry times 10,000 times, with every trade still paying its cost (wed-hztsQlQ); random sets of 200 ordinary days against the observed news-day loss.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Extend the permutation test used in P-0082: for each daily ETF strategy, draw random entry dates with matched holding period and exposure and report the share that beat the real result. For event-day ideas (C-05, C-06) draw random sets of ordinary days of the same size.

frameworks.name: Break-even win rate and the geometry check
frameworks.what_it_is: Before any backtest compute the win rate needed to break even, stop divided by stop plus target. A target five times closer than the stop hits first about five times in six whatever you do, so a high win rate is the starting line. Compare with random entries on the same bracket: if random does as well the signal is decoration. Check several brackets, not just the claimed one.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add break-even win rate and a same-bracket random-entry line to every report where a strategy has asymmetric stop and target or a limit exit (for example exits at yesterday's high). Treat any win rate above about 80 percent as a prompt to look for this.

frameworks.name: Pessimistic same-bar fill rule
frameworks.what_it_is: A bar gives open, high, low and close but not their order. When a bar touches both entry and target, or both stop and target, the optimistic assumption turns ambiguous bars into wins. Run both versions: optimistic, pessimistic (ambiguous counts as a loss) and a proven-wins-only count where the close is already beyond the target. Report the share of wins that come from ambiguous bars (65.7 percent in his test). The honest answer sits near the pessimistic one.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Daily bars have the same problem. Wherever a Proteus test uses a stop plus target, or fills at an intraday level such as a prior high, force the pessimistic order and report both. Add a switch to the shared backtest helper and log the gap between the two results.

frameworks.name: Cost stress and cost drag accounting
frameworks.what_it_is: Report edge per trade against cost per trade, and trades multiplied by cost (1,254 trades at 45 dollars was 56,430, more than a third of the whole loss in wed-hztsQlQ). Then stress: double or quadruple slippage and see whether the result survives; a one-tick change turned the runner-up on gold into a loser. In EruGJ-YIBWA doubling costs was one of four fragility checks, alongside nearby parameters, year-by-year splits and a frozen test.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: State the break-even round-trip cost in basis points for each ETF strategy and rerun at two and four times Proteus's assumed cost. Flag any rule whose edge per trade is below that.

frameworks.name: Profit concentration and decomposition
frameworks.what_it_is: Split results by day type (normal days versus trend days), side (89 percent of ORB profit from longs), year, month, and weekday. Report the share of profit from the best 10 percent of trades (nine times the total here), and the longest losing runs (seven months, nine days). Check whether any filter holds in both halves of the data; two of three filters flipped between periods.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add to the systems book report: top-decile trade share, long versus short split where relevant, worst month streak and a year table, so we can see whether a strategy is one fat tail in disguise and whether it would be survivable to run.

frameworks.name: Timing versus direction decomposition
frameworks.what_it_is: Take the exact moments a model chose to trade and swap its direction for a dumb rule; then run the dumb rule at all other moments. The model's direction made +170, the dumb rule at the model's moments made +10,900, the same rule elsewhere lost 155,655. Conclusion: the model knew when to stay out, not which way to go. Also sort trades by model confidence; the top 10 percent lost the most.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: For RSI(5) dip-buying, test whether the edge is in the entry timing (oversold days) or in being long at all: run the same dates with a plain buy-and-hold-for-N-days rule and the same exposure on non-signal days, and report each on its own line.

frameworks.name: Leak test by scrambling the future
frameworks.what_it_is: Deliberately scramble future data and check that none of the model inputs change; if a feature moves, it was peeking. Related: the pivot test in snZ89tkMFoA only lets a level trade after the right-hand confirmation bars have closed.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add a one-off test to every new signal function: shuffle all rows after bar t, recompute, and assert the signal at t is unchanged. Cheap insurance against lookahead in daily indicators.

frameworks.name: Event-study with a verified calendar and an event versus non-event control
frameworks.what_it_is: Build the event list from official sources, then verify each date against market behaviour (10-year Treasury futures volume about ten times normal in the first five minutes of a real release; this caught one wrong date, one holiday and several missing months). Exclude contract-roll days where they would distort a return. Measure events against random draws of ordinary days. Also note regime decay: reaction sizes differ by year, so an edge measured in 2022 may describe a market that has gone.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: For C-05 and C-06 build the Fed and jobs calendars once, check them against daily volume or range spikes in a Treasury ETF, and tabulate by year so a 2022-style outlier is visible.

frameworks.name: Rolling-window hot streak finder
frameworks.what_it_is: To see how a claim like 89 to 91 percent over 300 trades could arise, count the share of all possible 300-trade windows that reach the claimed rate (0.3 percent did), and which months they sit in. Also check the longest losing streak against the claim (five claimed, nine real).
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: When Proteus reads a claimed result from a short test window, compute how often a window of that length hits it in our own long daily history, and use the same to set expectations for the forward paper-trade of the RSI(5) book.

frameworks.name: Forward test compared with the backtest each week
frameworks.what_it_is: Treat a survivor of a thousand tests as a candidate. Trade it forward in small size and compare to the backtest every week; if behaviour drifts, assume the backtest was the liar. Choose position size so the worst drawdown is bearable (micro contract cuts drawdown from 93,465 to 9,410).
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Pre-register a divergence rule for the systems book: for example, a forward drawdown or hit rate outside a stated band of the backtest distribution for N weeks logs a kill or review line, decided before the first trade.

frameworks.name: Count the trials and state the limits
frameworks.what_it_is: Disclose that one survivor out of a thousand tests may be luck; that a Monday filter was found by looking at five weekdays; that random-basket tests do not fully correct for how many questions were asked; and that results rest on 39 to 208 events (LteukeidgbQ). Each video lists limits explicitly.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Keep a running trial counter in the track record (configurations searched, filters tried, weekdays or subperiods looked at) and print it beside each pass or fail, with a plain limits paragraph at the end of every probe write-up.
